body.text: A **large language model (LLM)** answers from its training and the context you give it. It may not know your current refund policy, last week's incident or a customer's private contract.
It can still answer confidently and wrongly. That's called a hallucination.

deepDive.title: What a language model knows, and what it does at question time

body.text: A language model is trained by adjusting many numerical **weights** so it gets better at predicting text. At question time, called **inference**, it uses those weights and the supplied context to produce the next tokens. A token is a piece of text, sometimes a whole word and sometimes part of one.

Training does not give the model a live connection to your document store. It may have learned an older public policy, never seen a private one, or learned patterns without reliably recalling the exact fact you need. A confident sentence is not a database lookup.

Suppose an employee asks, "What is our contractor equipment allowance?" The correct answer depends on the current company policy and that employee's access. General knowledge about typical allowances cannot answer that question safely.

There are two different problems here. **Knowledge access** asks whether the system can obtain the right current source. **Answer generation** asks whether it can explain that source accurately. Making a model larger might improve reasoning, but it does not automatically solve access, freshness or provenance.

RAG adds a knowledge-access path at inference time. The system finds relevant material and supplies it as context. The model's weights do not change when you upload a new document. The answer can improve because the evidence in the request changed. It still needs checks for whether that evidence is relevant, current and allowed.
**Retrieval-Augmented Generation:** before the LLM answers, search your own documents for the most relevant pieces and add them to the prompt. The model answers from those pieces and can cite them.
Think of it as an open-book exam for the model.

deepDive.title: Follow the documents from storage to an answer

body.text: **Retrieval-augmented generation** means generating an answer with material retrieved for the current question. It does not mean sending every document to the model, and it does not require a vector database in every design.

There are two linked workflows. Before a question arrives, ingestion reads source documents, extracts their content and prepares searchable units. A document might be a wiki page or a PDF. A **chunk** is a passage selected as one searchable unit. An index is a data structure that helps find useful passages without reading the entire collection on each request.

When a question arrives, the system checks the user's identity and permissions, searches for candidate passages, chooses useful evidence and builds the model request. The **prompt** includes instructions, the question and those sources. Generation turns the supplied material into an answer. A citation links a claim back to the source that supports it.

For "Can contractors claim a chair?", retrieval might return the contractor equipment section, including its furniture exclusion. The prompt supplies that section with a source ID. The answer can say the chair is excluded and cite the section.

These steps solve different problems. A perfect writing model cannot quote a rule that ingestion lost. A good search result cannot guarantee that generation preserves an exception. Evaluate both the evidence that reaches the model and the answer it produces. A useful first implementation can use keyword search; add other retrieval methods when measured misses justify them.
A user asks: "Can contractors expense a home office chair?"

items: Search finds 3 paragraphs from the Expense Policy.
The prompt becomes: instructions + those 3 paragraphs + the question.
The LLM answers: "No. Contractors aren't covered for office furniture (Source: Expense Policy, section 4)."

body.text: Nothing was retrained. Answers can reflect an updated policy once the new version is indexed and retrieved. How quickly that happens depends on your freshness design.

deepDive.title: Work through a question, evidence and a justified answer

body.text: Imagine the policy contains two nearby statements: "Contractors may claim approved equipment" and "Furniture, including chairs, is excluded." The question is, "Can a contractor claim a chair?"

Start by deciding **what evidence would answer the question**. A generic employee allowance page is not enough. You need the contractor rule and its furniture exception. The system should also know which policy version is current and whether this user can read it.

Retrieval returns possible matches. A candidate is not yet an answer: the top result might be an outdated page or a passage about employees rather than contractors. Selection keeps the current, permitted section containing both statements. If the passage was split before the exclusion, the context may misleadingly look like permission to buy a chair.

The context builder attaches a stable source ID and enough surrounding text to preserve the rule. The model can now answer, "No. The contractor policy excludes furniture, including chairs," with that source as its citation. A checker can verify that the cited text actually supports the exclusion.

Now remove the exception from the retrieved material. The safe conclusion is not to guess the allowance. The system should find the missing section, ask a useful clarifying question, or say it could not find enough evidence.

This example gives you a debugging order: inspect the source, extracted passage, selected context and final claim. Changing the prompt first would hide the real issue if the relevant sentence never reached it.

slides.title: When RAG is the right tool

body.text: Use RAG when:

items: answers depend on private or company data
the data changes often (docs, tickets, prices)
users need sources they can check
different users are allowed to see different documents

body.text: Skip it when the model already knows enough (general coding questions), or when all the data fits easily in one prompt.

deepDive.title: Choose retrieval because of the task, not because it is fashionable

body.text: RAG is useful when answers depend on an external source that must remain current, private or verifiable. Examples include an internal policy assistant, a support assistant that cites product documentation, or a tool that explains a particular customer's permitted records.

Ask four practical questions. Where does the answer live? How often does it change? Who may see it? Must the system show its evidence? If the source changes, an indexing update can make it available to later requests without retraining the generation model.

RAG has costs. Search can miss the right passage. Ingestion can lose table relationships. Retrieved text consumes context tokens, and retrieval adds latency and dependencies. You are building a knowledge pipeline, not merely adding one model call.

If the task is rewriting a paragraph that the user already supplied, retrieval may add no value. If all necessary material fits comfortably in the request, directly supplying it can be simpler. For an exact account balance or inventory count, query the authorized source of truth rather than treating a semantic passage match as an exact numerical lookup. Structured retrieval can still be part of a broader augmented assistant.

Try the simplest approach that meets the task. Test it on realistic questions, including missing answers and access restrictions. Add hybrid search, re-ranking or more elaborate indexing when you can name the failure they address. RAG improves access to evidence; it is not a guarantee that every generated answer is correct.

slides.title: RAG vs fine-tuning vs long context

items: **Fine-tuning** teaches a model a style, format or skill. It's a poor way to add facts that change, because you'd retrain every time.
**Long context** pastes whole documents into the prompt. Fine for a few files, but slow and expensive for thousands, and relevant details can be overlooked; measure this with your model and task.
**RAG** selects relevant pieces at question time. It can reduce context size and support citations, but adds retrieval work. Freshness and cost depend on the implementation.

body.text: Real systems often combine them.

deepDive.title: Separate changing behavior from supplying knowledge

body.text: Three mechanisms are often mixed together.

items: **Long context:** put the required material directly in the request. The model can use it immediately, but you pay to process that context and must stay within its usable context limit.

**RAG:** search an external collection and supply selected evidence. This helps when the collection is large, changing or access-controlled. Search quality and index maintenance become part of the system.

**Fine-tuning:** train the model further on examples, changing its weights. This can teach a style, output format or task behavior. It is not a dependable substitute for a database of frequently changing facts.

body.text: Suppose you need to summarize one uploaded report. Direct context may be enough. Suppose employees ask questions across millions of current documents with different permissions. Retrieval helps choose which permitted material belongs in each request. Suppose the assistant has the right evidence but repeatedly uses the wrong support-ticket format. Better instructions, examples or fine-tuning may address that behavior problem.

The choices can work together. A fine-tuned model can still consume retrieved sources, and those sources still occupy its context window. Fine-tuning does not remove the need to enforce permissions before supplying protected text. A long window does not mean the model reliably uses every passage in it.

Before choosing, describe the failure in plain words: missing knowledge, poor source selection, insufficient context, or the wrong response behavior. Then test the change against that failure instead of comparing product names.
An **embedding** is a vector: an ordered list of numbers representing learned patterns in text. Each number is a coordinate, called a **dimension**.
A 768-dimensional vector has 768 coordinates, not 768 words or named topics. Meaning is represented by the numbers together.

Related text can land nearby in this learned space. "Reset my password" may sit close to "I can't log in", even though the words differ. Similarity helps find candidates; it does not prove they answer the question.

deepDive.title: Read a vector without treating it as a fact or a permission

body.text: A **vector** is an ordered list of numbers. An embedding model maps text into such a list so that a chosen similarity measure can help find related text. Real text embeddings often have hundreds of dimensions. Individual dimensions usually do not have simple labels such as "finance" or "contractor."

For a toy picture, imagine a two-number representation. Two passages pointing in a similar direction can be near each other under cosine similarity. The actual model learns a much richer representation from training examples. The toy coordinates are an illustration, not real embeddings for those passages.

This is useful for paraphrases. "I forgot my password" and "reset account credentials" may share meaning without sharing many exact words. Searching embeddings can surface the second passage for the first question.

But related meaning is not the same as an answer. "Contractors receive an allowance" and "Contractors do not receive an allowance" can be very similar texts. The numbers alone do not prove which policy is current, whether the passage supports the claim, or whether the requester may see it.

Store a mapping from each vector to its original text, document version and access metadata. Search returns candidate IDs; the system retrieves the permitted text to inspect and pass to generation. Use compatible query and document encoders that produce vectors in the same learned space. Choosing a distance metric cannot repair a mismatched encoder pair or missing source evidence.
Two model roles work together:

items: **Embedding encoder:** text in, a vector of coordinates out. It prepares document vectors and encodes each question for search.
**Generative language model:** the question and selected passages in, a written answer out.

body.text: An encoder represents text for matching. A generator writes new text token by token. Both can use language-model architectures. Their sizes, speeds and costs depend on the models chosen.
In RAG, search selects useful passages. The generator reads their actual text and writes the answer.

deepDive.title: Why the embedding model and the answer model have different jobs

body.text: An **embedding model** turns text into numbers used for matching. A **generation model**, or LLM, produces text tokens conditioned on the material in its request. They may share some underlying techniques, but their outputs and serving jobs are different.

During indexing, the embedding service encodes document chunks and stores their vectors with links to the source text. This work can happen in the background. At question time, it encodes the query into a compatible space. The search system compares that query representation with the stored representations and returns candidate passages.

The generation model then reads selected passages as text. It does not usually reconstruct the documents from their stored vectors. The prompt builder supplies the actual source content, question and instructions. The model uses that context to produce an answer and source references.

For an equipment-policy question, the embedding service might help find the contractor section. The LLM's job is to preserve the rule and exception while explaining the result. If the search returns the wrong section, a more fluent LLM has not solved the retrieval error.

Choose and evaluate each part for its job. Retrieval needs a query/document encoding setup that works on your language and document types. Generation needs grounded answers at acceptable latency and cost. Updating an embedding model can require re-indexing documents; updating the answer model does not automatically require rebuilding every vector. Version both changes so their quality effects can be measured separately.

slides.title: The two halves of every RAG system

items: **Offline (indexing):** collect documents, split them into chunks, embed each chunk, and store the vectors plus metadata in a vector database. Runs ahead of time and again on every update.

**Online (answering):** embed the question, find the nearest chunks, build the prompt, call the LLM, and return the answer with citations. Runs on every question. Set and measure a latency target for the full path.

deepDive.title: Follow one update and one question through the two paths

body.text: The **offline path** prepares knowledge before it is needed. "Offline" here means outside the user's request, not disconnected from the internet. Connectors notice source changes, parsing extracts content and structure, chunking creates searchable passages, and embedding/indexing makes those passages searchable.

The **online path** serves a particular question. It authenticates the user, retrieves permitted candidates, optionally re-ranks them, builds context and generates an answer. A query should not normally wait for a complete corpus re-index.

Imagine a policy edit at 10:00. The source is current immediately, but search may still return the old indexed version until the change pipeline publishes a replacement. That delay is **freshness lag**. Give it a measurable deadline, then observe the age of the evidence used in answers.

An access revoke is a different promise. If a user's access is removed, a slow indexing worker must not be the only thing preventing disclosure. The query path needs a permission mechanism that meets the revoke deadline before protected content reaches the model. Cached retrievals and answers must respect that boundary too.

Store version information so you can explain which source, parser and embedding setup produced a result. When something is wrong, inspect whether the change was detected, processed and published, then inspect the query's selected version. The two-path diagram is useful because it separates a knowledge-maintenance failure from a question-serving failure; each needs different retries, metrics and recovery.

items: Support bots that answer from help-center articles
"Ask the wiki" assistants at work
Coding assistants that search your repo before suggesting code
Search engines that write a summary with links

body.text: If a chatbot shows its sources, there's a good chance RAG is behind it.

You now know what RAG is and when to use it. Next, you'll learn how each stage really works, and how interviewers test it, one topic at a time: from ingestion and chunking all the way to evaluation and safety.
By the end, you'll be able to design "ChatGPT for your company's docs" end to end, one of the most common AI system design interview questions.

questions.title: Why RAG
questions.prompt: What problem does RAG mainly solve?
options: LLMs don't know your private or recent data, so they guess
LLMs forget earlier turns in a long chat, so they lose track
LLMs answer too slowly, so search makes responses faster
LLMs can't follow formatting rules without extra examples
questions.keyIdea: RAG gives the model the facts it was never trained on.
questions.why: Without your documents in the prompt, the model fills gaps with plausible guesses.

ifWrong.1: That's conversation memory. RAG is about knowledge the model never had.
ifWrong.2: RAG adds a search step, so it usually adds a little latency.
ifWrong.3: Formatting is a prompting or fine-tuning job, not retrieval.

questions.title: Open book
questions.prompt: In a RAG system, what happens right before the LLM writes its answer?
options: Relevant pieces of your documents are retrieved and added to the prompt
The model is briefly fine-tuned on the matching documents
The whole document collection is pasted into the prompt
The question is matched to a cached answer from a past user
questions.keyIdea: Retrieve first, then generate.
questions.why: The model answers "open book" from the pieces it was handed.

ifWrong.1: Nothing is trained at question time. The pieces go into the prompt.
ifWrong.2: Only the top few relevant pieces fit and help. That's why we search.
ifWrong.3: A cache can sit in front of RAG, but RAG itself retrieves documents.

questions.title: Fresh docs
questions.prompt: Your expense policy changed this morning. What does a RAG system need so answers reflect the change?
options: Re-index the updated document
Increase the LLM's context window
Retrain the LLM on the new policy
Switch to a newer embedding model
questions.keyIdea: In RAG, fresh knowledge means fresh documents, not a new model.
questions.why: Re-indexing updates what search can find. The models stay the same.

ifWrong.1: A bigger window doesn't help if the new text never gets retrieved.
ifWrong.2: Retraining is slow and costly, and RAG exists so you don't have to.
ifWrong.3: The models are fine. The index still holds the old text.

questions.title: Fine-tune or RAG
questions.prompt: Which goal fits fine-tuning better than RAG?
options: Make the model always answer in your support team's tone and format
Answer questions about each customer's contract terms and renewal dates
Answer questions about this week's support tickets and their status
Cite the exact HR handbook section behind each answer
questions.keyIdea: Fine-tuning shapes behavior and style. RAG supplies facts.
questions.why: Tone and format are stable skills. Tickets, contracts and handbooks are changing facts that need sources.

ifWrong.1: Contracts are private facts that change. That's RAG.
ifWrong.2: Tickets change daily. Retrieval keeps up; fine-tuning can't.
ifWrong.3: Citations need the source text in the prompt. That's RAG.

questions.title: Two models
questions.prompt: Which statement about the embedding model and the LLM is true?
options: The embedding model turns text into a vector; the LLM writes the answer text
The LLM turns text into vectors; the embedding model writes the answer
Both are the same model, called in two different modes
The embedding model is the larger one, so it only runs at indexing time
questions.keyIdea: Embedding model finds, LLM writes.
questions.why: The embedding model maps text to vectors for search. The LLM reads the retrieved text and generates the reply.

ifWrong.1: Swapped. The embedding model makes vectors; the LLM writes.
ifWrong.2: They're usually separate models with different sizes and jobs.
ifWrong.3: It's usually smaller, and it also runs on every question.

questions.title: Meaning match
questions.prompt: "Reset my password" and "I can't log in" share no words. Why can vector search still match them?
options: Their embeddings are close because their meanings are similar
The search engine expands each query with a synonym list
An LLM rewrites every question before the search runs
Keyword search on word stems finds a shared root
questions.keyIdea: Embeddings capture meaning, not exact words.
questions.why: Similar meaning puts the two vectors close together, so search finds one from the other.

ifWrong.1: Synonym lists help keyword search. Vector search matches meaning directly.
ifWrong.2: Rewriting can help, but vector search matches these even without it.
ifWrong.3: They share no words or stems. Only meaning connects them.

questions.title: Count the vectors
questions.prompt: You index 1,000 documents, about 12 chunks each. How many embeddings do you store?
questions.keyIdea: You embed every chunk, not every document.
questions.why: 1,000 documents x 12 chunks = 12,000 vectors.

ifWrong.1: That's one per document, but search works on chunks.
ifWrong.2: Multiply, don't add. Each of the 1,000 documents has 12 chunks.

questions.title: Every question
questions.prompt: Which work happens on every user question, not ahead of time?
options: Embed the question, search for nearby chunks, then call the LLM
Re-embed the documents that match the question, then search
Split the matching documents into chunks, then call the LLM
Rebuild the vector index for the user's documents, then search
questions.keyIdea: Indexing happens offline; answering happens online.
questions.why: Chunking and embedding documents is done ahead of time, so each question only needs one embedding, one search and one LLM call.

ifWrong.1: Documents are embedded once, offline. Only the question is embedded live.
ifWrong.2: Chunking happens offline, before any question arrives.
ifWrong.3: The index is built ahead of time and updated when documents change.

body.text: A RAG system can only answer from what it retrieves, and it can only retrieve what ingestion stored.
If a table was mangled, a page was skipped, or a chunk cut a fact in half, no reranker or prompt can fix it later. Many "the model got it wrong" bugs in RAG are really ingestion bugs.

deepDive.title: See how an ingestion error becomes a wrong answer

body.text: **Ingestion** is the work that turns source material into the records your search system can use. It includes obtaining the document, interpreting its structure and publishing searchable content with its identity and permissions.

Consider a table with separate rows for employees and contractors. A parser drops the row labels but keeps the allowance amounts. Search now retrieves an amount without saying which group it applies to. The answer model may produce a fluent sentence, but the data supplied to it no longer preserves the policy.

There are several different failures to check. **Coverage** asks whether the document was ingested at all. **Fidelity** asks whether the extracted content still says the same thing. **Structure** asks whether headings, columns, lists and exceptions remain connected. **Freshness** asks whether the searchable version matches the current source. An index can contain every file and still fail the other three tests.

Keep source identifiers and versions throughout the pipeline so a returned chunk can be traced back to a page or section. Inspect representative outputs from PDFs, tables and long threads. Test questions that need an exception or a particular row, not only ones answered by a heading.

When debugging, compare the original with the extracted text before tuning embeddings. If a critical sentence is missing, a better similarity function cannot recover it. Repair the ingestion stage, rebuild the affected records and turn the failed example into a regression test.
Raw documents go through the same steps every time:

items: **Connect:** pull from sources like wikis, drives, tickets and chat.
**Parse:** turn files into clean text and structure.
**Clean:** strip boilerplate and remove duplicates.
**Chunk:** split text into pieces search can return.
**Enrich:** attach metadata to every chunk.
**Embed and index:** store vectors plus metadata.

body.text: Search returns chunks, not whole documents, so every step shapes what the model sees.

deepDive.title: Know what each ingestion step produces

body.text: A connector, parser and embedding service are not interchangeable. Each changes the representation of the document and should produce an artifact that you can inspect.

items: **Connect:** fetch the source content and its stable document ID, version and access information. Remember a checkpoint or change cursor so the next run can continue.
**Parse:** turn the file into meaningful blocks such as headings, paragraphs and table rows. A PDF's drawing commands or a scanned page are not already clean prose.
**Clean:** remove repeated menus and duplicate content while preserving substantive notes, exceptions and version information.
**Chunk:** group blocks into bounded retrieval units. Attach a parent document and section reference to each one.
**Enrich:** add the metadata needed for filters, permissions, citations and later updates.
**Embed and publish:** encode the text, store vectors with source links and make a complete document version available to search.

body.text: Suppose a worker fails after producing four of a document's ten chunks. Retrying must not publish duplicate chunks or expose a half-built version as complete. Use stable identities, record the processing state and publish only when the intended chunk set is ready. The exact transaction or version-switch mechanism depends on the stores you choose.

Not every edit requires every step. A permission-only change may update access metadata without re-embedding unchanged text. A parser upgrade may require rebuilding extracted content even when the source file has not changed. Version the processing configuration as well as the document.

items: **PDFs:** multi-column layouts, headers and footers repeated on every page, tables drawn as lines. Use a layout-aware parser.
**Scanned PDFs and images:** need **optical character recognition (OCR)** to turn pictures of letters into searchable text. OCR mistakes turn into search misses, so check the quality.
**HTML:** strip menus, ads and cookie banners. Keep headings and lists.
**Slides and spreadsheets:** keep the slide title or column headers with each piece of content.

body.text: Rule of thumb: read the parsed text of 20 real documents before you tune anything else.

deepDive.title: What OCR does, and why a PDF can still be wrong afterward

body.text: **OCR means optical character recognition.** It converts pictures of letters into machine-readable text. A scanned PDF may look like a normal document to a person while containing only page images. Searching those image bytes as if they were extracted words will not work.

A born-digital PDF may already contain a text layer. Try extracting that text and its positions. For scanned pages, an OCR path typically corrects orientation or skew, recognizes characters and returns text with locations. Mixed PDFs can need different handling on different pages. Do not assume the whole file has one representation.

Recognition is only part of parsing. A two-column page can produce all the correct words in the wrong reading order. A table can lose which price belongs to which plan. OCR does not automatically reconstruct those relationships. Use layout information to rebuild blocks, rows and headings before chunking.

For example, a scan might turn "100" into "l00", or attach a contractor allowance to the employee row. Those errors can change a policy answer, break exact-code search or corrupt a calculation. An LLM guessing the intended text is not reliable correction.

Compare extracted samples with the original pages across layouts, languages and scan quality. Check row associations, negative words such as "not", quantities and source page references. Route uncertain or unreadable pages to review rather than quietly indexing confident-looking mistakes. Keep the original reference so an answer's citation can lead back to the evidence that was actually parsed.
Real document sets are full of repeats: the same policy copied into five wikis, email threads quoting each other, old and new versions side by side.
Duplicates waste context tokens and push other useful results out of the top results.

items: Remove exact duplicates with a content hash.
Remove near-duplicates with a similarity check (for example MinHash).
Drop boilerplate such as repeated legal footers.
Decide early whether personal data must be removed before indexing.

deepDive.title: Remove repeated text without losing its meaning or access rules

body.text: **Exact deduplication** finds identical content, often by hashing a normalized representation. A content hash is a compact fingerprint: equal normalized content should produce the same fingerprint. Normalization might standardize whitespace, but it must not erase meaningful distinctions such as version dates or negative words.

**Near-duplicate detection** finds copies with small edits. For example, MinHash estimates overlap between sets of text fragments called shingles. It can identify mostly repeated pages without comparing every word of every pair. Similarity is evidence for review, not a reason to merge every related policy.

Why does this matter for retrieval? If five copied pages occupy the top five results, another passage containing an exception may be pushed out. Duplicate text also consumes embedding work, storage and prompt tokens.

Separate boilerplate from evidence. A navigation menu repeated on every wiki page is usually noise. A repeated legal exception might be essential. An email thread may quote an earlier message, but the new reply can change the conclusion. Inspect what your cleaning rule removes.

Also separate **content identity** from **source identity**. Two documents with identical text can have different owners or permissions. Sharing physical text storage must not combine their access rules or invent a public source. Preserve the source links, versions and authorization boundaries used at query time.
Evaluate cleaning on both retrieval quality and evidence preservation. A smaller index is not an improvement if it silently drops the paragraph that supports the correct answer.
**Chunking** splits a document into searchable passages called chunks. Each has an ID, source metadata and an embedding.
Three reasons:

items: Each embedding encoder has an input token limit; oversized text can be truncated or rejected.
One vector for a whole long document blurs many ideas into one point.
The LLM's context window is a budget. You want to send only the relevant parts.

body.text: Chunking gives each idea its own vector, so search can return just the paragraphs that matter.

deepDive.title: What a chunk is and why search needs one

body.text: A **chunk** is a bounded piece of a source document stored as a unit that search can return. It is usually a passage with its own ID, source reference and metadata. It is not just an arbitrary slice of characters, and it does not replace the original document.

Imagine a handbook covering hiring, leave and equipment. One vector for the whole handbook must represent many topics. Searching for a contractor's chair allowance may work better when the equipment section has its own searchable representation. The generation model then receives the relevant passage instead of the entire handbook.

Chunking serves three limits. The embedding model has a maximum input length. The representation must preserve enough detail to match the question. The answer model has a context and cost budget. Choosing a chunk boundary therefore changes both what search can find and what evidence generation can use.

A chunk should make sense outside its original page. "It is not covered" is a poor standalone result if the previous paragraph defined what "it" means. Keep a heading, subject or adjacent rule when it is needed to interpret the passage. Long tables and lists need special treatment because their meaning depends on structure.

Store a chunk-to-document link and the source version. That lets you fetch surrounding context, cite a section and remove or replace all affected chunks after an edit. You can search small units and supply larger parent sections later. There is no universal chunk size that makes every document self-contained.

items: **Too big:** the vector averages many topics, so matches get weak and tokens are wasted.
**Too small:** a chunk loses the context it needs. "It increased by 20%" means nothing without knowing what "it" is.

body.text: A common starting point is 200 to 500 tokens with 10 to 20% overlap. Overlap can preserve boundary context, but does not guarantee a whole sentence survives every split.
These are starting numbers. Pick the final size by measuring recall@k on real questions.

deepDive.title: Calculate overlap, then test whether it preserves the evidence

body.text: Chunk size and overlap control different things. **Size** limits how much content one chunk contains. **Overlap** repeats some content across neighboring chunks so information near a boundary is less likely to lose its context. **Stride** is how far the next chunk moves forward.

For fixed token windows, stride = size minus overlap. Consider exactly 1,000 tokens, a 200-token window and 40-token overlap. The windows start at 0, 160, 320, 480, 640 and 800. Six chunks store 1,200 token positions in total. The five shared boundaries repeat 200 tokens. This is a worked example, not a recommended production setting.

Tokens are not characters or words. Use the tokenizer and limits that matter for your embedding and generation setup. A character-based splitter needs its own checks rather than assuming every character count maps to the same token count.

Overlap is not a guarantee that a sentence stays whole. A long sentence, table row or rule-plus-exception can exceed the overlap. Larger overlap also increases embedding work, duplicate retrieval and context waste. If two adjacent chunks both enter the prompt, remove repeated spans when safe.

Compare candidate settings on labeled questions. Check whether the necessary evidence is retrieved together, whether the chunks remain understandable and how many tokens reach the prompt. For a contractor rule followed by a furniture exclusion, test the combined meaning rather than only whether the word "contractor" appears in a result. A structure-aware boundary or parent expansion may fix what extra overlap cannot.

items: **Fixed size:** split every N tokens. Simple and fast, but cuts sentences and tables.
**Sentence or paragraph:** split on natural boundaries. Better meaning, uneven sizes.
**Recursive:** try headings, then paragraphs, then sentences, until pieces fit the size limit. Compare it with a simpler baseline on your documents.
**Structure-aware:** follow the document's own sections, tables and code blocks.
**Semantic:** use embedding similarity to find possible topic boundaries. It adds compute; test whether the boundaries actually improve retrieval.

deepDive.title: Choose among chunking strategies by what creates a useful boundary

body.text: Chunking strategies differ in how they choose a cut. The goal is a searchable passage that still carries the evidence needed to answer a question.

items: **Fixed-size windows** cut after a chosen number of tokens or characters. They are easy to reproduce and cheap to run. Without other rules they can split a sentence, code block or table.
**Sentence or paragraph splitting** uses language boundaries. This often preserves a thought, but a very long paragraph can still exceed the model's limit and a short sentence may lack its subject.

**Recursive splitting** tries a hierarchy of separators. It keeps a large section when it fits, then tries paragraphs, sentences or smaller pieces when it does not. It is a size-control procedure, not proof that every cut is semantically correct.

**Structure-aware splitting** follows document elements such as heading paths, table rows and code functions. It is useful when those elements carry meaning, provided the parser recovered them correctly.

**Semantic splitting** compares neighboring text representations and cuts around apparent topic changes. It adds embedding work and a threshold to tune. Similarity changes can reflect wording rather than a meaningful boundary, so test it against a simpler baseline.

body.text: These approaches can be combined. Preserve a section heading, recursively split an oversized section and attach the heading to every child. Parent-child retrieval can then search the children but fetch a larger section for generation.

For a well-structured policy, start by preserving headings and exceptions. For messy prose, compare paragraph and recursive baselines. For code or tables, preserve their structure rather than forcing one generic window. Judge the result on realistic retrieval questions, evidence completeness, latency and storage, not on the strategy's name.

items: Keep each table with its header row, or turn each row into a sentence: "Plan Pro costs $49 for 10 seats."
Keep code blocks whole. Half a function is useless.
Keep list items with the sentence that introduces them.

Add the heading path to each chunk, like "HR Handbook > Leave > Parental leave", so the chunk still makes sense on its own. This is often called a contextual header, and it usually improves retrieval.

deepDive.title: Make a table row or list item understandable on its own

body.text: A parser can preserve every word while losing the relationships that give those words meaning. Chunking must preserve those relationships too.

Consider a table with columns **Plan**, **Price** and **Seats**. A chunk containing only "49, 10" cannot tell a reader what those numbers mean. One option is to preserve the complete table when it fits. Another is to render each row as a statement such as "The Business plan costs 49 units for 10 seats," keeping its column labels, section and source. The units and billing period belong with the value if the source supplies them.

The same issue appears outside tables. A list item may depend on an introductory condition such as "For contractors only." A code block may depend on its function signature or nearby explanation. A heading can identify the applicable country, product or year. Cutting away that context changes the evidence.

When structures are too large, split at meaningful subunits and repeat necessary context. For a long table, each child can carry the header and a range of rows. Preserve footnotes and exceptions that qualify those rows. Avoid inventing relationships when a scan or parser did not recover them confidently.

Test the extracted unit outside the original page: can someone tell who the rule applies to, what its values mean and where it came from? Then test retrieval questions that require the relationship. Merely matching a number or keyword does not show that the structure survived.
Small chunks match precisely. Big sections give the model enough context. You can have both:

items: Index small chunks (for example 150 tokens).
When one matches, send its parent section (for example 1,000 tokens) to the LLM.

body.text: A lighter version is the sentence window: match one sentence, then send the few sentences around it.

deepDive.title: Search a precise child, then fetch enough parent context

body.text: **Parent-child retrieval** separates the unit used for matching from the unit supplied to the answer model. A short child passage can match a focused question well, while its larger parent section carries definitions, conditions and exceptions.

At indexing time, assign children stable IDs and store a parent reference. A child might be a paragraph from the contractor equipment section. Its parent could contain the full rule and the furniture exclusion. Search the children, collect the matched parent IDs, deduplicate them and fetch the permitted parent content for the prompt.

This is not a reason to send unlimited parents. If ten children point to the same section, fetch that section once. If a parent is an entire handbook, expansion defeats the context budget. Choose a bounded parent, such as a subsection, or select a window around the match. A sentence-window variant retrieves a matching sentence and adds neighboring sentences.

Enforce source version and permissions on the fetched parent, not only on the child match. A cached child may point to an older document version. A parent can also include protected material beyond the matching passage. Do not accidentally widen what the user is allowed to see.

Measure whether expansion fixes incomplete evidence without adding too much unrelated text. The test is whether the answer preserves necessary context and exceptions. Small children plus large parents is a useful design option, not an automatic improvement over well-formed standalone chunks.
Store with each chunk: document ID, title, source URL, section path, author, created and updated times, version, language and access permissions.

items: **Filters** use it: "only 2026 docs", "only the billing product".
**Citations** use it: "Source: HR Handbook, updated Mar 2026."
**Freshness** uses it: prefer the newest version.
**Security** uses it: only return chunks the user is allowed to see.

body.text: The vector is only for matching. Anything you want to show or filter on must be stored next to it.

deepDive.title: Build a chunk record that can be searched, cited and replaced

body.text: The vector tells search about a representation of the text. It does not tell the application which document owns that text, which version is valid or who may read it. **Metadata** stores those operational facts alongside the searchable unit.

A useful record can include a stable document ID, chunk ID, source version, section path, language, tenant or access-policy reference, and the embedding/configuration version. A citation may also need a title, source URL and page or section location. Store only fields that have a clear job and that your privacy policy permits.

For example, document "equipment-policy", version 12, might produce child "equipment-policy:v12:contractors:2". The heading path identifies the contractor section. The version helps reject stale content. A parent reference supports expansion. An access-policy reference lets the serving layer apply the current permission rule.

Do not confuse **identity** with **content equality**. A content hash helps decide whether text needs reprocessing, but identical text can appear in different sources with different access rules. A row number alone is also fragile if edits insert earlier chunks. Choose identities that let a whole document version be replaced deliberately.

Treat access metadata from the source as authoritative input, not as a label inferred by an LLM. Define what happens when it is missing or stale. Verify that filtering, parent fetches, caches and citation links all use the intended boundary. Finally, keep the mapping needed to remove every chunk after a document is deleted.

An ACL is an access control list: the users or groups allowed to read a resource. Metadata can store a policy reference rather than copying every user ID, but serving still needs a current authorization decision.

items: Prefer change feeds or webhooks from the source over full re-crawls. Poll only when nothing else exists.
Track every chunk by document ID and a content hash. On an edit, re-embed only the chunks whose hash changed.
Publish a complete new document version, switch reads to it, then remove old chunks. An upsert alone may leave old chunks behind or expose a partial version.
Keep document versions, so you can tell old from new and roll back.

deepDive.title: Replace one document without exposing a half-built version

body.text: Freshness starts with **change detection**. A webhook or change feed can identify an updated document and its source version. Polling is a fallback when the source has no reliable feed. Keep a checkpoint and periodically compare source and index state, because events can be missed.

An edit can change the number and positions of chunks. Suppose version 12 has six chunks and version 13 has four. Upserting the four new chunks without retiring the old set can leave stale content searchable. Publishing chunks individually can also expose a mixture of versions while the worker is still running.

One design is to build a complete new version under separate versioned IDs, verify that it is ready, then switch which version reads may use. Retire the old set afterward. The switch might use a database transaction, an index alias or a serving-layer version check. Choose a mechanism that the actual stores support; do not assume a cross-store write is atomic.

Make processing **idempotent**: receiving the same event again should converge to the same published state. A stale worker must not overwrite a newer source version. Content hashes can avoid re-embedding unchanged text, while parser or encoder changes may still require a rebuild.

Measure the delay from source edit to searchable current evidence. Also check caches: a fresh index is not enough if an old retrieval or answer is still served. Keep versions in the request trace so a freshness report can be investigated.
A deleted document must disappear from search quickly. Process delete events by document ID and remove all of its chunks.
Permission changes matter just as much. If someone loses access to a document, their searches must stop returning its chunks.
Events get missed, so run a regular reconciliation job that compares the index with the source and fixes any drift.

deepDive.title: Handle revokes and deletes even when the ingestion worker is late

body.text: A source edit, a deletion and an access revoke have different safety requirements. An edit makes old content stale. A deletion may require the document to stop appearing. A revoke means this particular requester must no longer receive protected content, even if the text itself has not changed.

Suppose access is revoked at 10:00 and an index worker is delayed until 10:04. At 10:01, a search or retrieval cache may still return an old candidate. A serving-time permission mechanism must enforce the promised revoke deadline before that candidate's text reaches the answer model. That could involve current policy versions, a permission lookup or a safely invalidated authorization cache. The deadline determines what is acceptable.

Deletion also needs ordering. A delayed update must not recreate a document after a newer delete. A **tombstone** records the fact and version of deletion so older work can be rejected. Remove all chunk versions and clear or invalidate affected retrieval and answer caches. Keep only the minimal deletion marker required by your retention design.

If authorization cannot be checked reliably, do not send protected text and hope the prompt hides it. A citation link must enforce access as well. Parent expansion and cached answers belong in the same permission tests.

Finally, reconcile source and index state to catch missed events. Test both a cache hit and a fresh search immediately after revocation, plus a stale worker arriving after deletion. Saying "we filter by ACL" is incomplete without these timelines and failure behaviors.
When asked "How would you ingest the data?", cover these in about a minute:

items: Sources, connectors, and how you detect changes
Parsing per format, especially PDFs and tables
Chunking strategy and size, and how you'd tune it with recall@k
Metadata, including permissions
Updates, deletes and reconciliation

body.text: Bringing up deletes and permissions before you're asked is a strong Senior signal.

questions.title: Big chunks
questions.prompt: Why do very large chunks hurt retrieval?
options: One embedding averages many topics, so the match is diluted
Vector databases reject chunks over a few hundred tokens
Bigger chunks need more embedding dimensions to fit
The LLM can only read chunks shorter than 1,000 tokens
questions.keyIdea: One vector per chunk. The more ideas in a chunk, the blurrier its vector.
questions.why: Large chunks mix topics, so similarity to any one question drops, and they waste context tokens.

ifWrong.1: Vector stores hold fixed-size vectors. Chunk length doesn't change that.
ifWrong.2: The model's vector size is fixed. A long chunk gets the same number of dimensions.
ifWrong.3: LLMs read far more than that. The real issue is the blurry vector.

questions.title: Cut sentences
questions.prompt: You split every 300 tokens with no overlap, and a key sentence is cut in half. Best fix?
options: Add 10 to 20% overlap, or split on sentence boundaries
Switch to an embedding model with more dimensions
Double the chunk size to 600 tokens so cuts happen less often
Strip stop words so each sentence fits inside one chunk
questions.keyIdea: Overlap and sentence-aware splits keep ideas whole.
questions.why: Neither half of a split sentence carries the full meaning. Overlap repeats the boundary text in both chunks.

ifWrong.1: More dimensions can't rebuild a sentence that was cut in half.
ifWrong.2: Bigger chunks still cut sentences somewhere, and they blur the vector.
ifWrong.3: Removing words damages meaning and doesn't stop the cut.

questions.title: Split tables
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: Markdown docs are cut every 500 tokens, splitting a pricing table in the middle.
options: Rows lose their header row, so answers about the table come out wrong
500 tokens is too small a chunk size for Markdown files
Embedding models can't read Markdown table syntax, so tables are ignored
The table should be removed, since tables don't embed well
questions.keyIdea: Keep tables with their headers.
questions.why: A row like "Pro | 49 | 10" means nothing without "Plan | Price | Seats".

ifWrong.1: Size isn't the problem. Any fixed cut can split a table.
ifWrong.2: They can read it. The trouble is the rows that lost their header.
ifWrong.3: Tables hold key facts. Keep them with headers, or turn rows into sentences.

questions.title: Citation metadata
questions.prompt: Which metadata lets the answer show "Source: HR Handbook, updated Mar 2026"?
options: Title, source and updated timestamp
The chunk's embedding vector
The chunk's overlap and token count
The similarity score from the search
questions.keyIdea: Citations and freshness come from metadata, not from the vector.
questions.why: The vector is only for matching. Display info must be stored alongside it.

ifWrong.1: A vector is just numbers for matching. It can't be turned back into a title.
ifWrong.2: Those describe chunking, not where the text came from.
ifWrong.3: The score says how well it matched, not where it came from.

questions.title: Chunk count
questions.prompt: 2M documents, about 4,000 tokens each, 500-token chunks with 100-token overlap. About how many chunks?
options: 2M
questions.keyIdea: Chunks per doc is roughly doc tokens divided by (chunk size minus overlap).
questions.why: Each new chunk moves forward 400 tokens, so 4,000 / 400 = 10 chunks per doc, and 2M x 10 = 20M.

ifWrong.1: That forgets the overlap: 4,000 / 500 = 8.
ifWrong.2: That's one chunk per document.
ifWrong.3: That's 100 chunks per document. Each chunk adds 400 new tokens, so it's 10.

questions.title: Stale chunks
questions.prompt: Spot the flaw: when a document is edited, its new chunks are added but its old chunks stay in the index.
options: Old text still gets retrieved; replace a document's chunks by its ID
The embedding model must be retrained after every document edit to stay accurate
Edits should be ignored until a monthly full re-index
Overlap between old and new chunks causes duplicate vectors
questions.keyIdea: Updates must replace, not just add.
questions.why: Old chunks still match questions and return stale or conflicting answers.

ifWrong.1: The model is fine. The index still holds the old chunks.
ifWrong.2: That serves stale answers for weeks. Replace chunks on each edit.
ifWrong.3: Overlap isn't the cause. The old chunks were never removed.

questions.title: Changed chunks
questions.prompt: 100K documents are edited per day, 10 chunks each, and about 2 chunks actually change per edit. With chunk hashes, how many chunks do you re-embed daily?
options: 1M
2M
questions.keyIdea: Hash chunks and re-embed only what changed.
questions.why: 100K edits x 2 changed chunks = 200K.

ifWrong.1: That re-embeds every chunk of every edited document.
ifWrong.2: That's one chunk per edit. About 2 change each time.
ifWrong.3: That's 20 chunks per edit. Only about 2 change.

body.text: An embedding is a point in a learned vector space. Each number is one **dimension**, or coordinate. 768 dimensions means 768 coordinates; 1,536 means 1,536. Neither number counts words, documents or named concepts.

items: **Meaning is distributed:** many coordinates work together to represent learned relationships in text.
**Related text can be close:** "claim a chair" may sit near "furniture reimbursement" despite different words.
**Dimensions have a cost:** more coordinates need more storage, but do not guarantee better retrieval.
**Use compatible encoders:** different models' spaces cannot be mixed, even if their vectors have the same length.

deepDive.title: Dimensions are coordinates; meaning comes from the whole vector

body.text: A **vector** is an ordered list of numbers. Each position is a **dimension**, like each coordinate in a point on a map. A 2D point has two coordinates, such as [0.2, 0.8]. A 768-dimensional embedding has 768 coordinates. The number 768 is not a token count, document count or number of named topics.

An embedding encoder learns a representation from training examples. Its training objective encourages useful relationships, such as questions being close to passages that answer them. The resulting coordinates represent learned patterns jointly. One coordinate is not simply "finance" and another "employees"; meaning is distributed across many numbers and their relationships.

Use a deliberately tiny illustration. Put "claim a chair" at [0.20, 0.80] and "furniture reimbursement" at [0.25, 0.75]. Put "reset my password" much farther away at [0.85, 0.10]. Nearby points illustrate how different words can express related meaning. These invented coordinates are a teaching example, not outputs from a real model or human-named meaning axes.

Real embeddings need more coordinates to represent many interacting patterns. A model producing 1,536 dimensions uses twice as many coordinates as one producing 768, with corresponding raw-storage cost at the same numeric precision. More dimensions do not automatically mean better retrieval. Training, task fit and the data matter.

A fixed-length output also does not mean unlimited input. The encoder has its own token limit. A short question and a long passage can both produce 768 numbers while preserving different amounts of useful information.

Similarity remains fallible. "Contractors qualify" and "contractors do not qualify" discuss similar ideas but give opposite answers. Measure whether nearest passages support the actual question. Never interpret distance as truth, permission or a probability of correctness.
A metric defines how two vectors are "close". Direction means where they point; length means how far they reach.

items: **Cosine similarity:** compares direction while ignoring length. It ranges from -1 to 1; higher means more aligned.
**Dot product:** multiplies matching coordinates and adds them. Both direction and length affect it.
**Euclidean distance:** straight-line distance between the points. Lower means closer.

body.text: **Normalization** rescales vectors to length 1. Then cosine and dot product rank identically; Euclidean distance gives the equivalent reverse distance order.
Use the encoder's intended metric. A high score is not proof that a passage supports an answer.

deepDive.title: Choose a similarity measure that matches the encoder

body.text: A similarity metric compares two vectors. **Direction** is where a vector points; **length**, also called magnitude, is how far it reaches from zero. Different metrics use these properties differently, so "close" must have a defined meaning.
Use a toy query q = [1, 0] and two passages A = [1, 0] and B = [2, 1]. These invented coordinates show the math, not actual text embeddings.

**Cosine similarity** compares direction and ignores length. It is the dot product divided by the product of the lengths. A points in exactly the query's direction, so its cosine is 1. B points partly sideways, so its cosine is 2 / sqrt(5), about 0.89. Cosine ranks A first. The possible range is -1 to 1, not a probability scale.

**Dot product** multiplies corresponding coordinates and adds them. The query's dot product with A is 1; with B it is 2. It ranks B first because B's greater length outweighs its less-aligned direction. Raw dot product and cosine can therefore disagree.
**Euclidean distance** is straight-line distance between the points. Here A is distance 0 from the query and B is sqrt(2), about 1.41. Smaller distance is better; larger similarity is better.

**Normalization** divides a vector by its length so its new length is 1. For unit-length vectors, dot product equals cosine, and squared Euclidean distance equals 2 minus twice the cosine. They then give equivalent neighbor orderings, with distance reversed.

Use the encoder's intended metric and preprocessing. A high similarity only identifies a promising candidate. It does not show that a passage is current, authorized or supports the answer. Choose any no-answer threshold using labeled questions, not the appearance of a score like 0.89.
A **bi-encoder** has two independent text-to-vector paths: one for the question, one for a passage. They may share a model; "bi" does not require two different models.

items: During ingestion, encode passages once and store their vectors.
For each question, encode it once and compare with stored vectors.

body.text: This is fast because documents need not be encoded again for every search. The output is a matching score, not a written answer. The generative LLM later reads selected passages and writes text.
Independent encodings can miss fine query-passage details. Re-ranking can inspect shortlisted pairs together.

deepDive.title: Precompute documents, compare at query time

body.text: A **bi-encoder** is a retrieval architecture with two independent encoding paths: one for the question and one for a document passage. Each path turns text into a vector before the vectors are compared. The two paths may share model weights or use a jointly trained query/document pair. "Bi" does not require two different model products.

The document path runs during ingestion. For a million passages, compute a million vectors and store them in a search index. At question time, encode the new question once and search those stored vectors. You avoid reading and encoding every document again for every question.

That is its job in RAG: represent text for matching. The **generative language model** later reads selected passages and writes the answer token by token. Both can be neural text models and an embedding encoder can use a language-model backbone. The important distinction is the task and output: a searchable vector versus a generated answer.

For "Can contractors claim a chair?", the query encoder produces a vector. Search might return the contractor allowance and furniture exclusion. The answer-writing model receives their actual text and explains the rule with a citation. The vector itself is not the answer or a readable summary.

Independent encoding is efficient but loses some fine query-passage interactions. The document vector was made before anyone asked this particular question. It may blur "employees" versus "contractors" or miss a negation. A cross-encoder can inspect shortlisted query-passage pairs together to improve that ranking.
Keep the intended encoders, versions and normalization paired. A new query model cannot safely search an old index just because both vectors have the same length.
Judge models on your own data, not only on a public leaderboard like MTEB:

items: **Quality:** check whether the first k results include supporting passages for real questions.
**Domain and language:** legal, code, medical or multilingual text may need a specialized model.
**Max input length:** longer chunks get truncated or rejected.
**Dimensions:** more dimensions mean more memory and slower search.
**Cost and hosting:** an API priced per token, or self-hosted. Some data can't leave your network.

deepDive.title: Test the encoder on your own retrieval failures

body.text: Start with questions and the passages that would support their answers. Include abbreviations, exact identifiers, long sections, multiple languages and questions with no answer. Keep some examples out of model selection so repeated tuning does not simply memorize the test set.

Compare encoders on evidence retrieval at the shortlist sizes you can afford. Also measure query latency, ingestion throughput, storage size and supported input length. A strong short-passage model may silently truncate the exception at the end of a long chunk.

Use a small failure table. For "Does policy P-204 cover contractors?", record whether the current contractor section appears, its rank and any misleading older version. Inspect misses rather than choosing by one averaged benchmark number.

Version the encoder, tokenizer, normalization and chunking configuration together. Existing vectors remain in the old representation when you change the model. New query vectors cannot safely search them merely because both models output the same number of dimensions.

Before a migration, build a separate index and compare retrieval on the held-out set. A model that improves overall recall but loses a sensitive permission or language slice should not automatically replace the current one.
Raw vector memory = number of vectors x dimensions x bytes per number.

items: float32 = 4 bytes, float16 = 2, int8 = 1, binary = 1/8.
Example: 10M chunks x 1,024 dimensions x 4 bytes = about 41 GB.

body.text: A **vector index** is the search structure over the stored vectors. Its links or lookup tables add overhead, along with IDs and metadata.
Some models let you keep only the first part of each vector (Matryoshka embeddings), for example 256 of 1,024 dimensions, with a recall cost you must measure.

deepDive.title: Count raw vectors, then account for everything around them

body.text: Raw vector storage is **vector count × dimensions × bytes per value**. Keep the units visible so a dimension count does not accidentally become a byte count.

For 20 million chunks with 768 float32 values each, each vector uses 768 × 4 = 3,072 bytes. The raw vectors use 61.44 billion bytes, about 61.44 GB in decimal units or 57.2 GiB in binary units. "About 61 GB" is a reasonable rounded estimate if you state the convention.

This is not the total index or machine memory requirement. IDs, graph links or cluster lists, ACL metadata, deleted entries, text storage and operational headroom add space. Different index implementations keep different portions in memory or on disk. Measure a representative index rather than applying one universal multiplier.

Two full replicas double the storage for those copies. A blue-green embedding migration may temporarily need both old and new indexes as well. Copies are an explicit capacity decision, not free reliability.

If you propose lower precision, name the representation and test retrieval quality. The number of dimensions alone does not tell you bytes per vector. Keep vector capacity, document text storage and model-serving memory as separate estimates.
**Quantization** represents vector values with fewer bits. It saves space by keeping less numerical detail, not by deleting dimensions.
A 768-dimensional float32 vector uses 3,072 bytes. At int8, its 768 values use 768 bytes before scales and metadata. Approximation can change similarity scores and neighbor order.

items: **Scalar quantization:** encode each coordinate with fewer bits.
**Product quantization:** split coordinates into groups and store a code for each group's closest learned representative.

body.text: One option is compressed candidate search followed by higher-precision re-scoring. Include that extra copy in the memory budget. Test lost recall and latency on your data; there is no universal "small" quality loss.

deepDive.title: Compression trades numerical detail for a smaller index

body.text: **Scalar quantization** stores each coordinate using a lower-bit encoding. A toy example maps 0.146 to a nearby representable value such as 0.15. The error is small for that value, but two very close neighbors can swap order after approximation.

Rounding the printed number while still storing float32 does not save memory. The encoding must actually use fewer bits. For 768 coordinates, float32 takes 768 × 4 = 3,072 bytes; int8 takes 768 × 1 = 768 bytes before scales, identifiers and index overhead. The vector still represents 768 dimensions.

**Product quantization**, or PQ, compresses groups of coordinates. Imagine a group of eight float32 values, which uses 32 bytes. Train a codebook of 256 representative eight-value patterns. For each group, store a one-byte code selecting its nearest representative. The codebook is shared and also uses space. The group is approximated, not preserved exactly.

Search can estimate distances from those compact codes rather than reconstruct every full vector. Stronger compression can lose useful distinctions. The result depends on the corpus, codebook training and encoding settings, not just the compression ratio.

One serving design retrieves candidates using compressed vectors, then re-scores a shortlist with higher-precision originals. This may recover some ordering accuracy, but cannot rescue evidence absent from the shortlist. Retaining originals also reduces the total memory saving.

Compare against exact full-precision search and labeled answer evidence. Measure neighbor recall, evidence recall, latency and total storage, including codebooks and any original-vector copy. Do not delete arbitrary coordinates as a substitute: dimension reduction requires a method the encoder supports.
**ANN means approximate nearest-neighbor search.** It finds promising nearby vectors without comparing the query with every vector.
**Exact search** checks every eligible vector under the chosen metric. It finds exact neighbors, but that does not guarantee relevant evidence. Its work grows with the collection.
**Approximate search** explores a smaller part of the index. It can be faster, but may miss some exact neighbors. Graphs and clusters are two ways to reduce the search work.
If ANN finds 9 of the exact top 10 neighbors, neighbor recall@10 is 90%. Measure recall, latency and memory together. The next slides explain graph-based HNSW and cluster-based IVF.

deepDive.title: Approximate search needs a measurable reference

body.text: **Exact nearest-neighbor search** compares a query with every eligible vector under a chosen metric. It returns the exact nearest vectors for that representation. It does not guarantee the passages are relevant or factually correct.

**Approximate nearest-neighbor search**, often shortened to ANN, explores less of the collection to reduce work. It may miss some exact neighbors. The tradeoff is search speed and resource use versus retrieval accuracy.

For one test query, suppose exact search returns five IDs: A, B, C, D and E. ANN returns A, B, C, F and G. Neighbor recall@5 against that reference is 3/5. This differs from evidence recall, which asks whether the passages support a human-labeled answer.

Build an exact reference on a representative sample, then tune the ANN index against it. Measure latency under expected concurrency and with actual permission filters. Unfiltered single-query benchmarks can hide result starvation after access checks.

Exact search can be perfectly sensible for a small filtered collection or an evaluation baseline. ANN becomes useful when the measured cost of scanning eligible vectors is too high. Choose from observed workload needs rather than assuming every vector collection requires a complex index.
**HNSW means hierarchical navigable small world.** It is a graph-based ANN algorithm, not an embedding model.

Each node is a vector; links connect nearby vectors. Search follows promising links instead of checking every vector. Sparse upper layers move across the collection; denser lower layers refine nearby candidates.

items: **M:** links per node. More links cost storage and can improve connectivity.
**efSearch:** candidates explored per query. More exploration can improve recall at higher latency.
**efConstruction:** build effort. More effort can improve the graph but slows indexing.

body.text: Graph storage, filters and deletions depend on the implementation. Test recall and latency with your workload.

deepDive.title: Walk a graph from broad navigation to nearby candidates

body.text: **Hierarchical navigable small world**, or HNSW, is a graph-based ANN method. Vectors are nodes with links to nearby nodes. Sparse upper layers help move across the collection; denser lower layers refine the search near promising candidates.

Imagine finding a building using a few major roads first, then local streets. The search keeps candidates that seem closer to the query and explores their neighbors. It avoids visiting every vector, but a limited exploration budget can miss a better route.

Two settings matter conceptually. More links per node can improve connectivity while increasing storage and build cost. A larger search candidate budget explores more possibilities, often improving recall at the cost of latency. Names and exact behavior vary by implementation.

Graph links add memory beyond the vectors themselves. Updates, deletions, filtering and persistence also depend on the store. Check how your implementation handles deleted nodes and rebuilds; do not promise that deleting a row instantly removes every trace from every copy.

Tune on the queries and access filters you will serve. If strict filtering leaves few permitted neighbors, evaluate filtered recall and latency explicitly. A fast graph walk that returns no allowed evidence is not a successful retrieval.
**IVF means inverted file index.** It groups vectors into clusters and searches selected groups instead of the whole collection.
A clustering method such as **k-means** repeatedly assigns vectors to nearby centers and updates those centers. Each resulting list stores one cluster's vectors.
At query time, find nearby centers and scan their lists.

items: **nlist:** number of clusters. More clusters can shorten lists.
**nprobe:** lists searched. More probes can improve recall but add work.

body.text: A relevant vector in an unsearched list can be missed. IVF can combine with product quantization to save space. Measure actual memory, filtered recall and latency rather than assuming one index always wins.

deepDive.title: Search a few coarse clusters instead of the whole collection

body.text: An **inverted file index**, or IVF, partitions vectors into coarse clusters, often learned with a clustering method such as k-means. Each cluster has a representative centroid and a list of assigned vectors.

At query time, find nearby centroids and search their lists. If one million vectors are evenly split into 1,000 lists, probing 10 lists examines roughly 10,000 vectors before other optimizations. That is an illustrative average. Real lists can be uneven and filters can change the work.

Probing more lists generally improves the chance of finding exact neighbors but costs more search time. Probing too few can miss a relevant vector near a cluster boundary. Quantization can further compress the vectors within each list, introducing another quality tradeoff.

The coarse clusters must be trained on representative data. If new documents differ substantially from the training distribution, lists may become unbalanced or less useful. Monitor recall and list sizes as the corpus changes.

Compare settings against an exact reference and downstream evidence labels. Choose a probe count that meets quality and latency targets under load. The cluster count and probe count are tuning choices, not facts you can infer from document count alone.
Choose from the operations and workload you need:

items: **A vector library:** search algorithms; your application owns the surrounding storage and serving contract.
**A relational store with vector search:** can keep vectors, filters and transactional data together.
**A dedicated vector service:** compare filtering, durability, scaling and operating options.
**A search engine with vector support:** can combine lexical and vector retrieval.

body.text: Test current permissions, updates, deletes, backups, latency and index rebuilds. Capabilities depend on the implementation and deployment.
No tool is the right answer by name alone. State requirements, measure tradeoffs and justify the choice.

deepDive.title: Choose the operational contract, not a fashionable database

body.text: A vector library provides search algorithms. A production store may also provide durable writes, metadata filters, replication, backups and access control. These are different responsibilities; a fast benchmark does not prove the entire storage contract.

List the operations your RAG system needs: upsert a versioned chunk, filter by tenant and ACL, remove revoked content, fetch cited text, survive a node failure and rebuild after corruption. Give each an explicit freshness or availability requirement.

Then test candidates with a realistic corpus and query mix. A relational database with vector search can simplify transactions and joins. A dedicated search service may suit larger search workloads or particular filtering needs. A standalone library may work when your application owns persistence and updates.

For example, a great unfiltered ANN result is insufficient if an ACL filter takes too long or cannot meet the revoke window. Likewise, durable source text stored elsewhere needs a consistent mapping from search IDs to current versions.

Ask about backup restoration, rolling upgrades and index rebuild time before committing. Accept any justified implementation that meets the measured contract. There is no vendor name that replaces those checks.
Real queries almost always need filters: customer, permissions, product, date.

items: **Post-filtering:** take the top k, then drop what doesn't match. A strict filter can leave few or zero results.
**Filtered search:** apply the filter during the search, so all k results pass it. Most vector stores support this.
**Partition by tenant:** a separate index or namespace per customer. Strong isolation and easy deletes, but many small indexes to run.

body.text: Permissions belong in the search itself, never only in the prompt.

deepDive.title: Permission filtering changes the search problem

body.text: A **tenant** separates organizations. An **ACL**, or access control list, describes who may access a document. Both need to constrain retrieval. A tenant match alone does not authorize every employee to read every document in that tenant.

With post-filtering, a search might retrieve 20 attractive passages and discard 19 as forbidden. The one remaining passage may be insufficient even though useful allowed passages exist farther down the ranking. This is result starvation.

Filtering before or during candidate search can keep the search focused on allowed evidence. The available methods and performance depend on the index. Test whether the filtering path retains adequate recall rather than relying only on an API accepting a filter parameter.

Keep an authoritative permission check close to prompt construction when the index can lag revocations. A blocked passage must not enter the context, cache or citation preview. If permission verification is unavailable, do not silently fall back to an unfiltered search.

Create tests with users in overlapping and nested groups, an access revoke during a query and a warm cached result. Verify both non-disclosure and useful retrieval. Security and relevance must hold together.
A new model means a new vector space. Every document must be re-embedded; you can't mix old and new vectors.
A safe migration:

items: Build a second index with the new model in the background.
Write new and changed documents to both indexes.
Compare both on the same question set.
Switch reads with a flag, keep the old index for rollback, then delete it.

body.text: Store the model name and version with every vector, so a mismatch is caught early.

deepDive.title: Migrate embeddings without mixing incompatible spaces

body.text: Treat an embedding change as an index migration. The new query encoder and document representation must agree. Matching vector dimensions do not make two embedding spaces compatible.

Build a new versioned index while the old index continues serving. Backfill source chunks through the new encoder, recording source versions and a checkpoint. Apply new document changes to both paths, or replay a change log after the bulk backfill so updates are not lost.

Use shadow queries to compare retrieval without affecting the user's answer. Test relevance, permissions, deletions and latency. A migration that improves semantic matches but serves revoked documents fails even if its average recall rises.

Cut over the query encoder and index together. Keep a routing version so each request uses a consistent pair. Retain the old pair briefly for rollback and make sure rollback still respects current permissions and source deletions.

Budget the temporary storage and embedding throughput for both indexes. Re-embedding the whole corpus competes with daily freshness work and model quotas. A resumable batch job with idempotent writes is safer than restarting millions of chunks after one worker failure.
When asked "How would you store and search the vectors?", cover:

items: The embedding model and how you'd test it on your data
Vector count, dimensions and the memory math
The index type and its recall versus latency knobs
Filters and permissions inside the search
How you'd re-embed when the model changes

body.text: Showing the memory math ("10M x 1,024 x 4 bytes is about 41 GB, so int8 gets us to about 10 GB") is a strong Senior signal.

questions.title: Fast search
